body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Transition readiness assessment tools for adolescents with chronic conditions: a systematic review of measurement properties","authors":"Okonkwo-Harland B, Lindstrom-Achebe T, Vasquez-Pryce M","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Adolescent Health Care Transitions","doi":"10.5555/jahct.2020.0147","providerType":"review","abstract":"We identified 14 tools that assess readiness for transition from paediatric to adult care in adolescents with chronic conditions. Most were self-report checklists of disease knowledge and self-management skills, with parent versions for five. Content validity was rated adequate for eight tools and internal consistency for ten, but only three tools had been tested for whether scores predicted outcomes after transfer, and none in more than one condition. Few tools had been tested in young people with intellectual disability or in languages other than English."},{"title":"Does transition readiness predict outcomes after transfer to adult care? A prospective study in young adults with type 1 diabetes","authors":"Brennan-Nakashima L, Adeyemi-Castell R","year":2022,"venue":"Diabetes in Young Adults","doi":"10.5555/dya.2022.0063","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 286 young people with type 1 diabetes who completed a readiness questionnaire at 17 and transferred to adult care by 19. Readiness scores were not associated with HbA1c or clinic attendance 12 months after transfer (odds ratio for attendance per 10-point higher score 1.04, 95 percent CI 0.88 to 1.23). Attendance was higher among those who had met a named adult clinician before transfer. The authors suggest that readiness questionnaires describe skills rather than predict engagement and should not decide the timing of transfer on their own."},{"title":"Readiness as a process: young people's and parents' views of transition readiness questionnaires","authors":"Marchetti-Owusu E, Holmgren-Sato P","year":2019,"venue":"Child Health Experience Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held conversations with 21 young people with long-term conditions and 16 parents about readiness questionnaires used in two transition clinics. Young people felt the questionnaires tested knowledge they already had and missed what worried them, such as talking to new doctors and managing without their parents. Parents wanted their own changing role to be assessed. Both described readiness as growing confidence within relationships rather than a score, and several young people said a low score had delayed their transfer against their wishes."},{"title":"Structured transition programmes and attendance after transfer: a multicentre before-after evaluation","authors":"Achterberg-Fenwick J, Olatunji-Borg S, Kristensen-Ade N","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Adolescent Health Care Transitions","doi":"10.5555/jahct.2021.0288","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Six children's hospitals introduced a structured transition programme with a joint paediatric and adult clinic, a named transition coordinator and readiness checklists used as conversation tools rather than thresholds. Attendance at the first adult appointment rose from 64 to 82 percent, and loss to follow-up at one year fell from 21 to 12 percent. The programme had several components, so the contribution of readiness assessment cannot be separated from the joint clinic and the coordinator. Comparison hospitals were not included."},{"title":"Floor and ceiling effects of a 20-item transition readiness questionnaire across chronic conditions","authors":"Petrovic-Lindqvist A, Mensah-Hartley D","year":2017,"venue":"Paediatric Outcome Measurement","doi":"10.5555/pom.2017.0021","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed 1,940 completed readiness questionnaires from young people aged 14 to 18 with eight chronic conditions. Scores clustered at the top of the scale from age 16 onward, with 38 percent of 17-year-olds at the ceiling, so the questionnaire could not distinguish between older adolescents. Items about medication were answered very differently across conditions, and items about adult services were often skipped. The authors recommend condition-neutral items, a wider range of difficulty and caution in using scores to time transfer."},{"title":"Health literacy, deprivation and transition readiness scores in adolescents with long-term conditions","authors":"Kaur-Whitfield R, Obi-Marchand S","year":2023,"venue":"Child Health Equity Review","doi":"10.5555/chere.2023.0117","providerType":"cross-sectional study","abstract":"Among 512 adolescents with long-term conditions, lower readiness scores were associated with lower health literacy and with living in the most deprived areas, after adjustment for age and condition. Adolescents who needed an interpreter at clinic scored lowest, and the questionnaire was available only in English. The authors warn that readiness scores may partly measure literacy and social advantage, so using them as thresholds could delay transfer for disadvantaged young people. Scores were also lower when clinic letters went to a parent rather than to the young person, and the authors call for tools tested in several languages."},{"title":"Assessing readiness for transition in adolescents with intellectual disability: adapting a questionnaire for proxy and supported completion","authors":"Doyle-Nwachukwu H, Sandberg-Oyelowo M","year":2024,"venue":"Intellectual Disability and Health","doi":"10.5555/idh.2024.0035","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Standard readiness questionnaires could not be completed independently by most of 44 adolescents with intellectual disability in two transition clinics. An adapted version with pictorial items, supported completion and a carer section was completed by 40 of 44 adolescents and their carers. Carers valued questions about decision-making support and adult social care. The adapted version has not been tested for reliability or for whether it predicts outcomes, and the study was too small to compare adolescents with different levels of disability."},{"title":"Timing of transfer to adult services: age-based versus readiness-based criteria","authors":"Rahman-Castell T, Fairweather-Obi J","year":2016,"venue":"Paediatric Services Review","doi":"10.5555/psr.2016.0092","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared two clinics, one transferring at a fixed age of 18 and one transferring when a readiness score passed a threshold. Readiness-based transfer happened a median of nine months later, but one-year attendance and disease control after transfer did not differ between clinics. Young people in the readiness-based clinic more often reported frustration at staying in paediatrics. The clinics also differed in staffing and joint clinics, so differences in outcome cannot be attributed to the transfer criteria alone. Fewer than a third of young people in either clinic had met an adult clinician before transfer."}]}
